title: Democratic Backsliding
hook: Democracies rarely die in a single coup anymore. More often they erode — legally, gradually, step by step — until little is left but the shell of elections.
key_points: Backsliding is the gradual erosion of democracy, often by elected leaders themselves.
It typically works through legal steps, not a sudden coup.
Common moves: weakening courts, capturing media, sidelining opposition, changing rules to stay in power.
Each step can look minor, which is what makes the overall slide hard to resist.
content_html: For most of the 20th century, democracies that failed usually did so dramatically — a military coup, a violent takeover, a clear break. Democratic backsliding describes a quieter and now more common pattern: the gradual erosion of democratic institutions and norms, frequently carried out by leaders who were themselves elected. There is rarely a single moment when democracy "ends." Instead it is hollowed out from within while the outward forms — including elections — are kept in place.
extra_html: What makes backsliding distinctive is that it tends to proceed through legal or quasi-legal steps, each defensible on its own terms, which together shift a system toward authoritarian rule. The recurring moves are well documented by democracy monitors such as Freedom House: packing or weakening the courts so they no longer check the executive; bringing the media under control through ownership, pressure, or regulation; harassing, banning, or hobbling the opposition; and changing electoral rules, term limits, or constitutional provisions to entrench those in power. Because each individual step can be framed as lawful, necessary, or minor, opponents struggle to identify a clear line that has been crossed — and by the time the cumulative effect is obvious, the institutions that might have resisted have already been weakened. This is why backsliding is so dangerous and why analysts stress vigilance about the early steps: the erosion of judicial independence, press freedom, and fair competition matters not as isolated events but as the leading edge of a slide that is far easier to stop early than to reverse late.

source.name: Freedom House — Freedom in the World

related.title: Democracy vs Authoritarianism
related.hook: The deepest dividing line between regimes isn't left versus right — it's whether power can be lost. Can the people remove their rulers, or not?

related.title: The History of Democracy
related.hook: Democracy isn't a permanent gift — it's a hard-won, on-and-off achievement that nearly vanished for two thousand years before its modern comeback.

related.title: Electoral vs Liberal Democracy
related.hook: Holding elections isn't the whole of democracy. Without rights, courts, and limits on the winner, voting alone can deliver an elected strongman.

flashcards.back_html: The gradual erosion of democracy — often by elected leaders, through legal steps rather than a sudden coup.

flashcards.prompt: How does modern democratic backsliding most often occur?

choices.text: Through incremental, often legal steps by those in power
Almost always through a single dramatic military coup
By a foreign army occupying the country

flashcards.explanation_html: Contemporary backsliding typically advances by a series of lawful-looking moves rather than one overt seizure of power.

flashcards.prompt: Which is a characteristic move in democratic backsliding?

choices.text: Weakening courts, capturing media, and changing rules to entrench power
Expanding press freedom and fair competition

flashcards.explanation_html: Backsliding chips away at the checks — courts, media, fair competition — that would otherwise constrain those in power.
